opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't call it the ultimate summit, but I do think it's one of the most underrated layers. People often frame AI progress as a single axis: make the model smarter, a bit more capable at each step. When you look at how intelligence actually creates value in the world, though, it's rarely one brilliant individual working alone. It's many agents, human or otherwise, coordinating, dividing labor, checking each other's work, and building on shared context over long periods of time.

So there's a progression. First you need strong individual capability: reasoning, coding, long-context understanding. Then you need the ability to act, to use tools and carry out tasks over many steps. And once you have agents that can do meaningful work independently, the natural next question is how they work together. How do you get a group of agents to tackle something no single one could finish, like a large research project or running a complex software system end to end? That's where organizational capability comes in.

I'd still be careful about calling it the end point. Every time we think we've found the final layer, a new bottleneck appears. Better organization might expose limits in the base models, which pushes us back to improving pretraining or reinforcement learning, and the cycle continues. It's more like a spiral than a ladder with a top.

What I find exciting is that organizational capability might eventually be something the models learn rather than something we hand-design. Today a lot of multi-agent systems rely on human-written workflows: this agent plans, that one executes, another reviews. That's a bit like early machine learning with hand-crafted features. If the history of this field teaches anything, it's that letting the system learn the structure itself, given enough compute and the right objective, usually wins in the long run. So the interesting frontier isn't just making AI organizations, but making AI that can figure out how to organize itself.

r001.rationale: The response says it would not call organizational capability the endpoint, because new bottlenecks keep appearing and development continues in a spiral rather than ending at a top.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think I'd call it the summit, but I do think it's a very important stage, maybe the one people underestimate the most right now.

Let me explain how I think about it. If you look at the progression, the first stage was really about a single model being able to complete a single task. You give it a question, it gives you an answer. Then the next stage is agents, where a model can operate over a longer horizon, use tools, make decisions, correct itself, finish something that takes hours instead of seconds. That's roughly where we are now, and it's already changing how a lot of work gets done.

But if you think about how humans actually create value in the world, almost nothing significant is done by one person working alone. It's done by organizations. A company, a research lab, a team. The reason organizations exist is that there's a limit to what one brain can hold and do, so you need division of labor, coordination, shared context, memory that persists beyond any individual. So the natural next question is whether AI systems can form something like that. Not one agent that's very smart, but many agents that can plan together, split work, communicate, check each other, and accumulate knowledge over time.

What makes this hard isn't just scaling up the number of agents. A lot of the difficulty is in the things humans take for granted. How do you pass context between agents without losing information? How do you decide who does what? How do you handle disagreement, or an agent that's wrong and doesn't know it? How does the whole system learn from its own history instead of starting fresh every time? These are organizational problems, and I think they'll require new ideas, both in how the models are trained and in how the systems around them are designed.

So why don't I call it the ultimate summit? Because I think every time we reach a stage, we discover there's another one. Before agents, people thought a model that could do a task well was the goal. Then it became obvious that wasn't enough. I suspect the same thing will happen with organizations. Once you have AI organizations that work, you start asking about longer timescales, about things like an AI system that can run a multi-year research program, or sustain and improve itself in ways we haven't designed in advance. That's further out, and honestly I'm not sure what the right word for it is yet.

But in terms of what's actionable in the next few years, yes, organizational capability is where I'd focus. The thing I keep coming back to is that intelligence alone isn't the bottleneck for impact. Coordination is. A very smart individual with no ability to work with others is limited. The same will be true for models.

r001.rationale: The candidate says each stage reveals another and declines to call organizational capability the ultimate summit, suggesting AI development may have no final summit.

astra-6.text:
I’d hesitate to call it the ultimate summit. Organizational capability matters enormously, but I see it as the ability to keep making progress rather than as an endpoint.

In AI, you have to turn uncertain research into coordinated work. That means choosing which questions to pursue, getting people with different expertise to work together, and making sure experimental results actually change your decisions. A larger team or more compute doesn’t automatically give you that ability.

But organization can’t replace a good technical insight. Sometimes a very small team sees something everyone else has missed. The challenge is to build an organization that gives those insights room to emerge and can then execute on them. So I’d say organizational capability and technical judgment have to develop together.

r001.rationale: The response frames organizational capability as a way to keep making progress rather than an endpoint, indicating that AI development need not have an ultimate summit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think organizational capability is very important, but I wouldn’t necessarily call it the ultimate summit. It’s what allows a group of people to keep solving difficult problems together, rather than depending on a few individuals or a single breakthrough.

In AI, you need research, engineering, and product development to reinforce one another. The organization has to help information flow between those teams and make it possible to change direction when an assumption turns out to be wrong. That matters especially when there isn’t an established playbook.

But organizational capability still has to serve a purpose. A very efficient organization can pursue the wrong technical direction. So I’d put the emphasis on whether we can keep discovering what matters, turn those discoveries into useful systems, and learn from the results. Organization is a crucial part of that process, but it isn’t the endpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says organizational capability is not the endpoint, but does not claim that AI capability development as a whole may have no ultimate summit.
